title: Retrouvailles au Grand Colbert  (Reunion at Grand Colbert)

segments.t: At Le Grand Colbert restaurant, Mathias finally arrives to meet Annick and their daughter Camille. Years of estrangement create palpable tension as the former couple exchange polite pleasantries and order drinks. Listen to the conversation in French first.
J'ai besoin d'un verre. Garçon!
Regarde maman, il est là.
Il n'a pas changé.
Toi non plus.
Bonjour Annick. Bonjour Camille.
Bonjour Mathias.
Vous n'allez pas vous serrer la main?
Non, bien sûr que non.
Asseyez-vous, Mathias.
Un homme important doit être pressé.
Oh, vous savez...
Juste un café, s'il vous plaît.
Et un verre de rouge pour moi.
Je m'en occupe.
Vous vous occupez de tout, toujours.
Mieux vaut tard que jamais.
Let's walk through the conversation step by step.
J'ai besoin d'un verre. Garçon!
'I need a drink. Waiter!' Annick signals the server to cope with her nerves. The traditional noun addresses brasserie waiters.
Regarde maman, il est là.
'Look Mom, he is here.' Camille spots her father entering the brasserie. The adverbial particle pinpoints physical presence in the room.
Il n'a pas changé.
'He has not changed.' Annick observes Mathias with quiet surprise after eight years. The negative compound past tense notes his familiar appearance.
Toi non plus.
'Neither have you.' Camille offers an encouraging compliment to her mother. The adverbial phrase non plus expresses agreement in the negative.
Bonjour Annick. Bonjour Camille.
'Hello Annick. Hello Camille.' Mathias greets them with formal reserve. The standard greeting introduces the awkward family reunion.
Bonjour Mathias.
'Hello Mathias.' Annick responds cautiously, maintaining polite distance. The mutual formal tone highlights years of silence.
Vous n'allez pas vous serrer la main?
'Are you not going to shake hands?' Camille points out their stiff physical hesitation. The reciprocal construction se serrer la main questions their formality.
Non, bien sûr que non.
'No, of course not.' Mathias declines the cold corporate gesture between past lovers. The fixed emphatic expression reinforces obvious negation.
Asseyez-vous, Mathias.
'Sit down, Mathias.' Annick invites him to join them at the table. The reflexive imperative asseyez-vous conveys formal courtesy.
Un homme important doit être pressé.
'An important man must be in a hurry.' She uses gentle irony about his busy life. The adjective describes someone short on time.
Oh, vous savez...
'Oh, you know...' Mathias deflects the remark with understated modesty. The conversational filler avoids boastful agreement.
Juste un café, s'il vous plaît.
'Just a coffee, please.' Mathias orders a quick hot beverage from the waiter. The polite courtesy phrase completes the beverage request.
Et un verre de rouge pour moi.
'And a glass of red wine for me.' Annick chooses wine to steady her emotions. The elliptical phrase un verre de rouge designates red wine colloquially.
Je m'en occupe.
'I will take care of it.' Mathias offers to cover the order. The pronominal verb s'occuper de expresses handling a responsibility.
Vous vous occupez de tout, toujours.
'You take care of everything, always.' Annick evokes his habitual need for control. The pronoun tout functions as direct object of the action.
Mieux vaut tard que jamais.

'Better late than never.' Mathias acknowledges their belated family reunion. The traditional French proverb reflects on timing and reconciliation. Now listen to the whole scene again at normal speed, and see how much more you catch.

Mieux vaut tard que jamais.
Mathias and Annick attempt to bridge eight years of distance over coffee and wine, under the watchful gaze of their daughter Camille. Listen to the French conversation one more time.
C'est bon de vous voir.
